articles.title: FinMin examining suggestions for changes in equity capital gains tax: CBDT
articles.summary:
The Finance Ministry is examining various aspects of capital gains tax on equities, and probable changes in taxation would come in the Union Budget for 2027-28, a senior official said on Monday.
Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) Chairman Ravi Agrawal said the ministry is considering suggestions from various stakeholders made during the pre-budget meetings.
"We will consider it, and I'm sure on February 1 you will get to know. Analysis is being done of whatever issues have been flagged or points that have been raised by the stakeholders," Agrawal told reporters on the sidelines of the inauguration of a CBDT lounge at the IITF here.
Agrawal said the different facets of the capital gains tax regime, including tax implications, will be examined, and the decision will be announced in the Budget.
Industry chambers have already made representations to the Ministry recommending abolition of Long Term Capital Gains tax (LTCG).
They also suggested rationalising short-term capital gains .

articles.title: India's sugar output more than doubles to 2.35 mn tonnes by Nov 15: ISMA
articles.summary:
India's sugar production more than doubled to 23.59 lakh tonne in the ongoing 2026-27 season through November 15, as mills in top producer Maharashtra started crushing early, the Indian Sugar & Bio-Energy Manufacturers Association (ISMA) said on Monday.
Output stood at 11.49 lakh tonne in the same period a year earlier, the industry body said. The sugar season runs from October to September, with crushing typically starting in October-November.
The sweetener's production in Maharashtra, the country's biggest producer, jumped more than threefold to 18.51 lakh tonne from 5.25 lakh tonne a year earlier. Mills in the western state began crushing from October 8, earlier than in other states, and 154 mills were operating as of November 15, against 132 a year ago.
Output in Uttar Pradesh, the second-biggest producer, fell to 2.10 lakh tonne from 4.25 lakh tonne, with 80 mills operational compared with 88 a year earlier.
In Karnataka, the third-largest producer, output was little changed .

IBM spends about USD 3 billion annually in India and plans to invest USD 10 billion globally in quantum computing over the next five years, Chairman and Chief Executive Arvind Krishna said, underlining the technology major's long-term commitment to the country even as he flagged significant disruption to employment from artificial intelligence.

articles.title: Belrise Industries shares jump 11% as Q2 profit rises 25% YoY; revenue grows 17%
articles.summary: Belrise Industries shares rallied 10.50% to Rs 237.78 during Monday’s trading session after the company reported 25% year-on-year (YoY) growth in profit after tax (PAT) and a 17% increase in revenue from operations for the September quarter (Q2 FY27).Belrise Industries Limited (BIL), an integrated automotive component manufacturer, announced its financial results for Q2 FY27 and the first half of FY27, reporting growth in both revenue and profitability.The company's revenue from operations increased 17% YoY to Rs 2,746 crore in Q2 FY27, compared with Rs 2,353 crore in the corresponding quarter of the previous financial year. Profit after tax (PAT) rose 25% to Rs 166 crore from Rs 133 crore in Q2 FY26.Belrise Industries Q2 FY27 business highlightsThe company's manufacturing revenue grew 26% YoY to Rs 23,441 million in Q2 FY27, compared with Rs 18,601 million in the year-ago quarter. Manufacturing EBITDA increased 19% to Rs 3,170 million from Rs 2,663 million in Q2 FY26. Manufacturing EBITDA margin stood at 13.5% during the quarter. Additionally, 71% of the company's manufacturing revenue came from powertrain-neutral products.Belrise Industries H1 FY27 performanceFor the first half of FY27, manufacturing revenue increased 23% YoY to Rs 45,420 million, compared with Rs 36,923 million in H1 FY26. Manufacturing EBITDA rose 15% to Rs 5,963 million from Rs 5,199 million in the corresponding period last year. The manufacturing EBITDA margin stood at 13.1%, while powertrain-neutral products accounted for 71% of manufacturing revenue.Belrise Industries secures new ordersDuring the quarter, Belrise Industries secured several new orders across its commercial vehicle and two-wheeler and three-wheeler businesses. The company won a programme from a leading Indian commercial vehicle manufacturer to supply complete chassis frame assemblies across its heavy commercial vehicle (HCV) platforms. The supplies will be made from a new facility in Dharwad, with production expected to ramp up from Q1 FY28.The programme is expected to add Rs 60,000–1 lakh in content per vehicle, with peak annual revenue potential of Rs 1,500–2,000 million.Belrise also entered complete three-wheeler body manufacturing after being selected as the second source for complete body and chassis assemblies for a high-selling model of a leading Indian two-wheeler and three-wheeler manufacturer. The order represents incremental content of approximately Rs 9,000 per vehicle.Production from its new facility at Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar is expected to ramp up from Q1 FY28, with peak annual revenue potential of Rs 1,000–1,200 million.In its suspension business, the company onboarded its sixth original equipment manufacturer (OEM) customer, a leading premium two-wheeler manufacturer in South India. Supplies commenced in Q3 FY27. It also secured additional orders from a growing two-wheeler and three-wheeler OEM, with production expected to begin in Q4 FY27.What management saidCommenting on the company's Q2 and H1 FY27 performance, Shrikant Badve, Managing Director of Belrise Industries, said the quarter was marked by strong execution and a healthy demand environment. He highlighted that manufacturing revenue grew 26% YoY to Rs 23,441 million, while adjusted PAT increased 25% to Rs 1,663 million.Also read: Tata Motors PV shares crack 9% as Motilal Oswal cuts earnings estimates, stays bearish after Q2 resultsThe company also secured its maiden Letter of Intent (LoI) for the supply of CNC fixtures to an ecosystem partner of one of the largest American smartphone companies.According to Badve, India's electronics manufacturing ecosystem is poised to become one of the country's largest and most cost-competitive manufacturing segments. The new order will provide Belrise with an opportunity to demonstrate its precision engineering capabilities developed over the years.Share PriceBelrise Industries shares have rallied 45% over the past one year. articles.title: Inox Wind shares tumble 10% as Q2 margins disappoint, CEO resigns. Why Motilal Oswal cut target price, earnings estimates

Additionally, the company announced the resignation of its CEO Sanjeev Agarwal, effective immediately.Inox Wind shares dropped to Rs 58.01 apiece on NSE on Monday morning. This comes after the renewable energy player reported a consolidated net profit of Rs 58.83 crore for the July-September quarter of the ongoing financial year 2027, marking around 36% year-on-year decline from Rs 91.75 crore reported in the corresponding quarter of the previous financial year.The company’s revenue from operations increased more than 21% YoY to Rs 1,354 crore during the quarter under review, from Rs 1,119 crore reported in the same period last year. Total expenses meanwhile increased more than 28% YoY to Rs 1,275 crore. Also Read | India Inc’s Q2 profit jumps 26%; auto, financials, oil & gas lead growthInox Wind’s EBITDA dropped more than 22% YoY to Rs 238 crore, from Rs 306 crore in Q2 of FY26, with the EBITDA margin slowing to 17%. The company however said this does not reflect the true picture as income from wind world O&M portfolio has not been recognised in the earnings for this quarter. The company’s management acknowledged that the earlier FY27 guidance of around 75% YoY revenue growth is unlikely to be achieved and has shifted its focus to FY28, with revenue guidance of Rs 7,500 crore.Additionally, Inox Wind announced that its CEO Sanjeev Agarwal has resigned due to personal reasons, while former Vikram Solar CEO Saibaba Vutukuri has been appointed as the Managing Director of of Inox Wind’s wind business.Motilal Oswal on Inox Wind share priceMotilal Oswal Financial Services reduced its target price for Inox Wind shares to Rs 74 apiece, while maintaining its ‘Buy’ rating on the stock. The target price implies around 15% upside potential from the stock’s previous closing price of Rs 64.45 apiece on NSE.The domestic brokerage said the company’s consolidated revenue came in 7% above estimates, while EBITDA missed expectations by 5%. It noted that WindWorld’s acquisition, 3.8GW order book providing over 24 months of execution visibility, supplemented by a healthy 5 GW near-term tender pipeline, and recurring opportunities from Inox Clean Energy are some of the things it liked from the earnings print.Motilal Oswal however noted that the lowering of guidance, timely consolidation of WindWorld from Q3 FY27 and execution of margin improvement initiatives, as well as benefits from the strategic shift toward equipment supply need to translate into lower working capital intensity and improved cash conversion, are the key monitorables. The domestic brokerage cut FY27 and FY28 EBITDA estimated for Inox Wind by 21% and 14% respectively, factoring in lower estimated deliveries and moderated EBITDA margins of 18% and 19%.Also read | Jefferies' Chris Wood sees fresh US-Iran tensions as biggest risk to India, sees this sector as the best hedgeInox Wind share priceInox Wind shares dropped more than 11% in a week and nearly 13% in one month, with the stock overall being down around 52% in 2026 so far and 60% in one year. In the longer term, Inox Wind shares have fallen more than 5% in three years but delivered positive returns of more than 78% in five years. Jimmy Tata accuses Noel of 'backdoor takeover'
articles.summary: Jimmy Naval Tata, younger brother of late Ratan Tata and one of the longest-serving trustees of Sir Ratan Tata Trust (SRTT), has accused Noel Tata of using the charitable institutions to consolidate family control over Tata Sons, calling the induction of multiple family members into the trusts a “back-door takeover” of the group’s holding company.In a detailed written response to a senior trustee on the state of affairs at Tata Trusts and controversies surrounding the group, Jimmy has also criticised changes to Tata Sons’ Articles of Association, backed chairman N Chandrasekaran’s reappointment and called on the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to enforce the listing of Tata Sons without delay.Also Read: Jimmy Tata breaks silence on Tata matters; backs Chandra staying chair & Tata Sons listing, opposing Noel's stance“What has transpired in recent time is that the trusts are being filled with family members of the present Tata Trust Chairman, thereby securing a degree of control over Tata Sons that was never the settlors’ intention,” he said, adding that having more than one family member on a trust was inappropriate.“Such an arrangement is untenable and amounts to a back-door takeover of Tata Sons,” he said.Jimmy’s intervention is significant as the 85-year-old trustee has largely stayed away from trust meetings and voting and has rarely publicly articulated his views on the ongoing differences within the group.He said the two principal Tata trusts were established by Sir Ratan Tata and Sir Dorabji Tata for public welfare and that trustees were custodians of their assets, not owners. He cited their founding objectives, including poverty alleviation and safeguarding Indian culture, and said the institutions should remain focused on serving the people of India.Jimmy traced the current governance differences to amendments made to Tata Sons’ Articles of Association around 2013-14, which he said had fundamentally altered the relationship between the charitable trusts and the operating company.He argued that the earlier framework kept the welfare trusts separate from Tata Sons’ commercial operations, while subsequent amendments gave the Tata Trusts chairman veto powers and the ability to place directors, undermining the collective authority of the board.He also questioned differences in trustee tenure rules, alleging that they had compromised independence and enabled the marginalisation of dissenting trustees.Also Read: Noel Tata warns Tata Sons listing could put profits ahead of philanthropy, says it may change the ‘Tata way’Citing Venu Srinivasan, whose term expires in December, he alleged that Srinivasan was being targeted for opposing the induction of Noel Tata’s son into SRTT. He also referred to the earlier removal of Vijay Singh.Jimmy contrasted the current situation with the past, when independent figures such as Nani Palkhivala, Gautam Sarabhai, Homi Sethna and Homi Bhabha served as trustees.On the differences over Chandrasekaran’s continuation as Tata Sons chairman, Jimmy praised his leadership, saying he had turned around companies burdened by severe debt and delivered record earnings and substantial dividend payouts.“Despite Chandrasekaran receiving overwhelming support (including 4–1 in Tata Sons board and a unanimous resolution passed by Tata Trusts), Noel sought to block him arbitrarily by invoking the onerous veto provisions in the amended Articles of Association without providing any justification or accountability,” he said.Jimmy’s comments come amid a widening rift between Noel, chairman of Tata Trusts, and the Tata Sons board over Chandrasekaran’s reappointment, the proposed listing of the holding company and the group’s governance structure.Tata Trusts collectively owns about 66% of Tata Sons, with SRTT holding 23.56%. Its position is central to decisions concerning the future of the holding company and the wider conglomerate.Jimmy said listing Tata Sons was critical to improving transparency and accountability and restoring the separation between the charitable trusts and the commercial operations of the group.“Listing would dismantle the pervasive culture of secrecy, impose statutory accountability, and necessitate rewriting the onerous Articles of Association to restore the pre-1989 separation between business operations and welfare trusts,” he said.He also warned against any attempt to restructure Tata Sons into smaller entities to avoid regulatory listing requirements, saying this would be contrary to public and shareholder interests.Jimmy called on the RBI to enforce strict timelines for listing and urged the government and the Charity Commissioner to intervene to protect the original objectives of the trusts.The RBI has classified Tata Sons as an upper-layer non-banking financial company (NBFC), requiring it to list its equity shares on a recognised stock exchange within three years of being identified in that category. The central bank has rejected Tata Sons’ application to surrender its core investment company registration, requiring it to comply with the regulatory framework applicable to upper-layer NBFCs.Also Read: Tata International appoints T V Narendran as Chairman and Noel N Tata as Chairman Emeritus effective November 12Jimmy has been a trustee of SRTT since 1989 and is one of its three perpetual trustees, the others being Noel Tata and Jehangir Jehangir. He is the younger son of Naval Tata and his first wife Sooni Commissariat. Noel Tata is Naval Tata’s son from his second marriage to Simone Dunoyer.Jimmy, who lives in Pune, has historically preferred correspondence to participation in trust meetings. During a 2016 interview, he showed reporters a file containing hundreds of letters through which he had communicated his views to trustees and board members.He is also the second-largest individual shareholder of Tata Sons after Noel Tata, with a 0.81% stake, or 3,262 shares, according to estimates based on investment banking data.

articles.title: FPI buying hits 5-year high in November. What's driving the $7.5 billion inflow?
articles.summary: Mumbai: In a sharp U-turn after months of sustained selling, foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) pumped $7.5 billion into Indian equities in the first 10 trading sessions of November - the highest monthly inflow in five years, according to Bloomberg data.This comes after FPIs withdrew $2.17 billion from Indian equities in October and $3.46 billion in September. The net investments in November so far are the highest since November 2021. The last time foreign investors pumped in more money in a single month was November 2020, when inflows stood at $9.56 billion, the data showed.135868866According to fund managers, FPIs have been aggressively investing amid a correction in AI-related stocks globally and a decline in crude oil prices. "The FPI flows are driven by multiple factors. profit booking on AI Investments, drop in oil prices, election results in Brazil, correction in Indian valuations over last two years, talks of exemptions on capital gains and reduction in rupee volatility," said Nilesh Shah, managing director of Kotak Mahindra AMC.All this came in quick succession and the combined effect is visible in FPI flows, he said.Read more: IPO calendar: Mahanadi Coalfields among 3 companies to raise over Rs 10,000 cr in busy week for primary marketBrent crude prices have fallen nearly 21% to $93.37 per barrel on November 13 from a peak of $118 on October 30. The Indian rupee has appreciated by ₹1.97, or about 2%, against the US dollar since the beginning of October, rising from ₹96.22 per dollar to ₹94.25 per dollar by mid-November.Domestic institutional investors, meanwhile, have turned net sellers, booking profits amid a sharp rally in the market, after providing a crucial backstop through much of the year. DIIs have sold equities worth over ₹49,000 crore in the first 10 trading sessions of November, according to NSE data. Since the beginning of November, the Sensex and Nifty have gained nearly 10% each, while the BSE MidCap 150 and BSE SmallCap 250 indices have advanced around 8% each.Read more: Will Sensex, Nifty continue their bull run or consolidate? 4 factors to watch out for this weekOverseas investors began 2026 with net outflows of $3.26 billion into Indian equities in January, before turning net buyers in February with investments of $1.69 billion. However, the respite was short-lived, as March saw a sharp reversal, with FPIs pulling out $13.23 billion - their biggest monthly sell-off.Their return to Indian equities reflects both global portfolio rotation away from AI-heavy markets and improving outlook for India, said Anurag Byas, director for global markets solutions at Rothschild & Co. "Lower crude prices, better earnings and now attractive valuations seem to have supported this sentiment change. This is a positive signal but may be early to be extrapolated; the fundamentals must improve and the oil and currency stability must hold for this to become a sustained trend," he said. Shah of Kotak Mahindra AMC expects FPI flows to move in line with how the above factors interplay with each other.

articles.title: Dems should call Trump’s immigration bluff
articles.summary: In casting their ballots for Democrats, voters couldn’t have been clearer about their disgust with Republican Party priorities — including, as even President Donald Trump has admitted, his administration’s overzealous approach to immigration enforcement. “It might be too tough,” he told 60 Minutes last Sunday. Yet Trump has been anything but clear when asked what he plans to do about it.This past week alone, the president has veered from offering to work with Democrats on immigration reform to defending the promotion of immigration hard-liner Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff. Trump said targeting immigrants without criminal records “hurt” Republicans, but also said he’s not making changes. “There won’t be amnesty,” he told reporters. And that’s on top of his administration bragging about hitting new records for deportations. “Thanks to President Trump’s leadership,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said, “ICE has been unleashed.”ALSO READ | More companies may face action in H-1B probe, warns US Labour Department's Anthony D’EspositoGiven all the mixed messages, it seems highly unlikely that a fix for the nation’s broken immigration system is coming if Trump gets to dictate the agenda and the timetable. To be sure, a compromise would be ideal. But if anything is to get done on immigration in the next Congress, Democrats will likely have to force the issue, pushing legislation and daring Republicans to filibuster it or Trump to veto it.Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has proposed just such a strategy for making health care more affordable. Trump will have two choices, as Schumer told the Washington Sun. He will either sign what will be very popular legislation — “and he’ll know it’s popular” — or obstruct it, giving Democrats a better chance of winning the presidency in 2028.ALSO READ | IBM's H-1B move, US tech layoffs: Why is it getting harder for Indians to work and settle in America?The same could work for legislation on immigration reform (although it doesn’t seem to be a priority for the House so far). The key for Democrats will be resisting the temptation to go too far left, as some in the party want to do, and instead stick to policies that match public opinion and stand a good chance of improving the economy.Polls show that most Americans appreciate the economic benefits of legal immigration. They want a secure border, but don’t approve of violent enforcement tactics that have left multiple people dead. Americans also favor admitting refugees and asylum seekers fleeing war-torn countries, and providing a viable pathway to citizenship for immigrants who were brought to the US as children, or have been living in the US for years.Depending on the day, Trump will pay lip service to agreeing to much of this. As he told 60 Minutes last Sunday, killers should be deported, but not necessarily “good people working in a landscaping company or working in a hotel” and “paying taxes.”But Trump has said such things before, only to backtrack. He did so in 2017, when he toyed with helping DREAMers — immigrants brought to the US as children — get citizenship. What had seemed like a more solid deal fell apart in 2018 after immigration hard-liners, led by Miller, got involved. Another one fizzled in 2019.Trump has never been a particularly reliable negotiating partner. He breaks promises and changes his mind on a whim. With Miller in Trump’s ear more often now as White House chief of staff, Democrats are right to be skeptical that will change just because Republicans received an electoral beatdown for the ages. Yet Democrats seem to be moving forward anyway, however tentatively.This past week, a group of Latino lawmakers, many of them newly elected to Congress, gathered outside the Capitol to publicly push for immigration reform. Specifically, they called on Trump and Republicans to support the bipartisan Dignity Act and the American Dream and Promise Act, both of which would solve a mix of problems with the current immigration system.“I have very aspirational dreams and hopes for immigration reform. But I am also a pragmatist,” Representative Veronica Escobar of Texas said. “And as we have — as we continue to have — Donald Trump in the White House, and without a supermajority in the Senate, we need Republican support. So any comprehensive immigration reform must be bipartisan.”Senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona said congressional Democrats had a responsibility to “protect as many families as possible,” even if that means “potentially cutting a deal with Donald Trump.”A smaller group of Latino business leaders who also spoke at the Capitol were more direct and, dare I say, more realistic. They reminded the Trump administration that its policy of mass deportations has disrupted the economy, forcing businesses to close and workers to stay home, forfeiting their paychecks. This has been as true in the Rio Grande Valley of Texas as it has been in southwestern Kansas. And it had a lot to do with Republican Latino voters abandoning Trump.In a warning to the administration, Benny Melendez, vice chair of the South Texas Builders Association, said to nods from Latino lawmakers: “If you want to continue harassing our communities, prepare yourself not only to lose your job, but get ready, because in the 2028 elections, these same communities you are now harassing will make sure you lose the White House.”The reality is, Trump may never compromise on legislation. That shouldn’t stop Democrats from advancing a vision of what a well-run immigration system could look like, and explaining how that could ease everything from the housing shortage that’s driving up costs to labor shortages at meatpacking plants and farms that threaten to raise grocery prices even more.If Democrats can present a plan that’s in line with what most Americans want, there’s a good chance voters will reward them for it — and punish Republicans for standing in the way. Just because the Trump administration is in disarray over immigration doesn’t mean Democrats have to be as well.The views expressed in this article are the author's own and do not necessarily reflect the views of the publication.

Delhi AQI dips to 290, but relief may be brief
articles.summary: Following days of toxic, post-Diwali smog blanketing the national capital, Delhi's air quality improved slightly to the 'poor' category on Sunday, with the Air Quality Index (AQI) reaching 290 by 4 pm.Across the city's 58 monitoring stations, 34 registered 'poor' air quality and 23 logged 'very poor', leaving only Delhi Cantonment in the 'moderate' zone. NSIT Dwarka recorded the capital's worst air, with an AQI of 364. Earlier that morning, the Sameer app had placed the city's air in the 'very poor' bracket at 350.Per the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) scale, an AQI of 0–50 is 'good', 51–100 is 'satisfactory', 101–200 is 'moderate', 201–300 is 'poor', 301–400 is 'very poor', and 401–500 is 'severe'. Delhi had been stuck in the 'very poor' tier continuously since November 11, with hourly readings repeatedly nearing, and once breaching, the 'severe' threshold. Prior to Sunday, the last 'poor' AQI reading was 299 on November 10, preceded by 261 on November 1.Real-time PM2.5 source apportionment data from the Air Quality Early Warning System and the Integrated Decision Support System identified biomass burning, encompassing stubble burning, domestic solid biofuels, wood, and dung cakes—as Sunday's primary pollutant source at 37.1 per cent. Secondary organic aerosols, which are fine particulates generated by atmospheric gas reactions, ranked second at 22 per cent, trailed by vehicular emissions (17.2 per cent) and secondary inorganic aerosols (9.6 per cent). Smaller shares came from waste burning, such as municipal, plastic, and rubber waste (5.5 per cent), mixed combustion (4.3 per cent), mineral dust and ash (2 per cent), firecrackers (1.6 per cent), and industrial emissions (0.6 per cent).This relief is expected to be brief. According to the Air Quality Early Warning System, Delhi's air will likely stay 'poor' on November 16 before deteriorating back to 'very poor' on November 17 and 18, remaining in that bracket for the following six days.Meteorologists credited Sunday's temporary dip in pollution to light rain and stronger winds helping disperse trapped pollutants. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) noted that parts of Delhi experienced drizzle or very light rain over the preceding 24 hours, accompanied by southwesterly surface winds peaking at 15 kmph. Skies were mostly cloudy before turning partly cloudy by afternoon, with southwesterly winds blowing up to 10 kmph.However, the IMD's forecast bulletin projects the city's ventilation index to drop steadily, from 16,000 square metres per second on November 15 to 15,000 on November 16, 7,500 on November 17, and 6,000 on November 18. The bulletin noted that a ventilation index below 6,000 square metres per second, combined with average wind speeds under 10 kmph, creates poor conditions for dispersing pollutants.

articles.summary: Dhaka: Fresh labour unrest hit Bangladesh's garment industry on Sunday, with 13 factories shut indefinitely and five others declaring a one-day holiday, a day before the wage board is due to meet to continue consultations on recommending a revised pay structure.Protesting workers gathered in Gazipur's Konabari and Mouchak areas, prompting police to use tear gas and sound grenades to disperse them. Factory owners said 50 units in the industrial zone were closed.Also Read: Floppy disks, paper strips and ageing computers: America's aviation system is stuck in the pastThe latest disruption comes amid weeks of protests over workers' demand to raise the minimum monthly wage from 12,500 taka (USD 100) to 30,000 taka (USD 240), with demonstrations and factory shutdowns reported across key industrial belts.Bangladesh is the world's second-largest garment exporter after China. The sector employs more than four million workers and accounts for over 80 per cent of the country's export earnings, making prolonged disruption a concern for international buyers and global supply chains.Also Read: Ebola outbreak remains out of control in Congo 6 months into responseThe government formed a Minimum Wage Board on November 1 to recommend a revised pay structure. The board, chaired by a senior district judge, agreed at its first meeting to finalise its recommendations by the end of November.The revised pay structure is expected to take effect from December 1, with workers set to receive their first salaries under the new scale in January.The fresh unrest on Sunday came a day after garment factory owners warned of indefinite, unpaid closures at factories where workers refused to resume production.Police and factory owners said 13 readymade garment factories were shut for an indefinite period, while five others declared a one-day general holiday in Gazipur and nearby Ashulia.Workers at a garment factory rallied in Gazipur's Konabari area, prompting police to rush to the scene and disperse them using tear gas and sound grenades at around 8.30 am local time.Workers from other factories later took to the streets in the adjacent Mouchak area, forcing management to close their units."Workers made attempts to gather at different locations this morning, but law enforcement personnel prevented them with their prompt actions and remain deployed at every key point in the industrial area," Gazipur Industrial Police Superintendent Amzad Hossain said.Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) said it had deployed 13 platoons of paramilitary personnel to maintain order and protect factories, alongside police in riot gear and the elite Special Response Battalion (SRB), which draws personnel from the army, navy, air force and police.Gazipur district administration officials said several platoons of the Ansar battalion had also been called out to guard the factories. They said 25 executive magistrates had been assigned to lead law enforcement personnel.Factory owners said 50 garment units were closed in the industrial zone, including 13 shut on Sunday amid fresh unrest.Officials said production continued at most factories in Gazipur's industrial belt despite the disruption.The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) said its representatives would attend the minimum wage board meeting on Monday to submit their proposal, despite reluctance among some of its members.The BGMEA, however, warned that its participation in subsequent meetings would depend on how the situation on the ground unfolded.The continued protests have centred on demands for a "living wage to survive", with workers saying their earnings have not kept pace with rising costs of food, housing, transport and healthcare.Factory owners have warned that prolonged disruption during the peak production season for spring and summer orders could delay shipments, affect overseas buyers' confidence and lead to cancellations.Bangladesh supplies major international fashion brands, including H&M, Zara and Gap. The sector has also faced pressure from rising production costs, inflation and intense competition in global markets.The protests turned violent in the first week of November, with demonstrators setting ablaze police vans and public transport vehicles and blocking two major highways.Ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) activists also took to the streets in anti-protest campaigns, carrying bamboo sticks to maintain order and resist what they described as "infiltrators".BNP leaders have accused Hasina and her supporters of trying to destabilise the government through the protests, while the former prime minister has rejected such allegations in media interviews.Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's information affairs adviser, Zahedur Rahman, earlier accused the deposed premier of fuelling the unrest, saying, "Sheikh Hasina will not let the government remain in peace as long as she is alive".A student-led uprising toppled Hasina's government on August 5, 2024, forcing her to flee to India. The interim government led by Muhammad Yunus later disbanded the Awami League under anti-terrorism legislation.

Unlike the abrupt crashes that have punctuated previous crypto downturns, much of the preceding decline unfolded during relatively subdued trading before liquidations accelerated in recent days.The steady erosion is adding to a sense of exhaustion across a market confronting a growing list of obstacles, from the record hack at Binance and renewed political uncertainty following Democratic gains in the US midterm elections to rising Treasury yields and a stronger dollar. Meanwhile, the artificial-intelligence boom and Anthropic’s upcoming IPO are competing for money and attention once directed toward digital assets.“The near-term direction will largely depend on whether institutional demand stabilizes and macro conditions provide room for risk appetite to recover,” said Ayesha Kiani, chief operating officer at Monarq Asset Management. “Until then, rallies are likely to remain fragile and volatility elevated.”135852805US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, which helped draw Wall Street investors into the market, have become another source of selling pressure. From Oct. 30 — the day after the Binance hack — through Nov. 13, the ETFs saw almost $3 billion in net outflows.Economic conditions offer little relief. The yield on 10-year US Treasuries has climbed above 5% as persistent inflation fueled expectations of tighter Federal Reserve policy. Higher yields raise the opportunity cost of holding assets that generate no income, while the stronger dollar has added pressure to Bitcoin and gold.Crypto-specific developments have compounded the weakness.The Binance hack has revived questions about the security of trading platforms at a time when the industry is struggling to rebuild investor confidence. The competition for speculative capital is also intensifying. Anthropic’s planned initial public offering has attracted heavy demand ahead of its expected listing, raising the possibility that investors are freeing up money from other holdings, including cryptocurrencies, to participate. The extent of any direct shift out of digital assets remains unclear.“Theories around the market weakness tend to focus on the large outflows of stablecoin balances, nearly $20 billion over the last month, the upcoming IPO of Anthropic and its impact on liquidity,” said Joshua Lim, co-head of markets at FalconX.Bitcoin’s retreat is particularly frustrating for investors who had expected mainstream adoption to provide a more durable foundation for prices. Major financial institutions have expanded their involvement in digital assets, and ETFs have made Bitcoin available to a much broader pool of investors. Those advances have not insulated the market from its latest downturn.Many smaller digital tokens have surrendered years of gains, challenging the returns available to investors who held through successive industry booms and busts.For traders looking for a potential floor, August offers one reference point.After risk appetite improved following the US Treasury’s announcement of an increase in long-bond buybacks, Bitcoin rallied from below $65,000 to above $87,000 by late September. The latest decline has erased most of those gains and raised the prospect of a further slide under the roughly $58,000 level that has marked this year’s low.“We’re in a risk-off environment across all financial markets. Interest rates keep rising with the war still pressuring inflation,” said Ryan Watkins, co-founder of crypto investment fund Syncracy Capital.

articles.title: Glare falls on US's antiquated aviation infra
articles.summary: The major disruption in US air traffic, which affected thousands of passengers and flights, started with a seemingly small incident. A glitch during an upgrade of the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) telecommunications infrastructure cascaded into widespread flight cancellations and delays, stopping America in its tracks for hours and hours.Amid a frantic race to contain the fallout from this dramatic embarrassment, something far less dramatic has drawn public attention: ageing wires, outdated routers and technology that belongs to another era running a modern system.Also read | What passengers need to know as flight disruptions continueAs America counts the costs of the disruption, the world's gaze has fallen on how the most advanced of economies was brought to its knees not by natural calamity, a terror attack or an aircraft shortage, but by a weak link in its infra.Old, antiquated systemsThe November 13 happenings exposed one thing more than anything else -- the fragility of America's ageing air traffic control (ATC) communications network.The question being asked now is, how can the country that leads the world in technological innovation still depend on decades-old systems to keep its skies safe?A country that has put astronauts in space should not have to worry about whether its air traffic controllers can communicate with an aircraft because a decades-old router has stopped behaving, yet that is the uncomfortable reality staring in America's face, as the system running the world's largest aviation infra is showing its age more and more, Reuters reported.According to FAA's accounts, the disruptions were triggered by a communications failure involving a router during an upgrade. But the incident is about much more than one faulty tool.Also read | 20,000 flights hit as FAA's ageing technology faces a fresh test after suspected router failureMore than anything, it has shown what the increasing fragility of an ageing system can lead to.It has put the spotlight on the risks of replacing critical infra while it is still in operation, and the possibility that another seemingly minor technical glitch could bring American aviation to a standstill again, with enormous economic and potentially disastrous safety fallouts.The big challengeThe episode has brought to the fore a very difficult test of modernisation.The FAA is trying to replace a network that has evolved over decades without interrupting communications. This is a critical matter, because all aircraft operations depend on these communications.In the November 13 incident, systems contractor L3Harris was changing old copper telephone connections to fibre-optic lines when the trouble began.Newly installed routers reportedly generated more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, destabilising communications across 17 of the FAA's 22 en-route air traffic control centres, Reuters reported.The routers being replaced are around 25 years old and were originally due for replacement in 2006.The bill for maintaining the old network comes to around $1 billion a year. More than 70% of the planned conversion has been done. The rest of the work will have to be completed while the system remains in service, which, by FAA's own account, can be quite a challenge.135849512A much deeper problemThis router failure was only the most visible symptom of a much bigger, deeper problem.On November 5, the FAA announced that it had begun replacing floppy disks used to store weather and other essential information at more than 400 air traffic control facilities.Floppy disks are a relic from a time long gone by.The new Enterprise Information Display System is intended to replace four separate systems dating back to the 1980s, with the transition expected to be fully done by the end of 2028.What is more, the agency also continues to rely on decades-old Compaq computers and sources replacement components through eBay.These computers were from another era, and are not made anymore. The company that made them was acquired by HP in 2002.Even a planned end to using paper flight strips, which controllers still use to track aircraft, remains unfinished. In aviation circles, this is often a butt of jokes. A programme was started in 2022 to bring in digital alternatives at 49 major airports, but it remains unfinished, and will likely take until at least 2028.According to various reports, this represents a striking picture of technological neglect in a country that is otherwise at the forefront of digital innovation.Cautionary talesIndications are that the November 13 disruption will hardly be the last such case. The FAA's own accounts tell several cautionary tales.In January 2023, a contractor accidentally deleted files in the agency's Notice to Air Missions system, forcing a nationwide ground stop lasting 90 minutes and disrupting around 11,000 flights.*In September 2026, a circuit failure at a Philadelphia air traffic facility and the accidental cutting of a fibre-optic cable by a construction crew in New Jersey disrupted thousands of flights across the densely populated Northeast.**The takeaway is that aviation systems are only as strong as their weakest links. A minor installation error, damaged cable, malfunctioning component or software problem can quickly escalate and affect many airports, airlines and airspace.When such things happen, the authorities, as an immediate response, restrict traffic or stop departures to maintain safety. But the cascading disruption thereafter stalls planes, strands flyers, cuts off cargo movements and inflicts huge costs on airlines, airports and other businesses.To be fair, these vulnerabilities are not unique to America. In a similar recent case, Greece had an eight-hour radio communications outage (January 4, 2026), forcing authorities to clear the country's airspace and divert dozens of planes. A probe later identified outdated communications infrastructure, including equipment no longer supported by manufacturers, as part of the problem.***But these cases become more eye-catching coming from America, the world leader in everything tech.135849523Financial falloutThe financial fallout of such US aviation shutdowns is usually enormous.The US air transport system is the backbone of passenger & business travel, tourism and time-sensitive freight. A prolonged disruption can cause a chain reaction of missed flights, aircraft/crew displacement, stalling of valuable cargo, cancellations and delays that can continue long after the original fault has been addressed.More importantly, passenger safety cannot be compromised just to keep flights moving.If controllers can't access reliable radar information and communications, cutting traffic or grounding planes becomes unavoidable, causing major damage not just in money but also in the form of hours wasted.The US govt is seized of the enormity of the task. Congress has okayed $12.5 billion for air traffic control modernisation, while Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is pushing for another $50 billion for aviation infrastructure and airports.However, according to industry people, funding alone is unlikely to solve the problem.Among other things, the FAA must make sure new systems can integrate with old infra without destabilising either of them, while at the same time building enough redundancy into the critical communications system, Reuters reported.*, ** and *** source: Reuters and AP reports

articles.summary: Markets regulator Sebi will soon issue detailed guidelines for the responsible use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the capital markets, its chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said, emphasising the need to balance technological innovation with investor protection.The Sebi chief said the proposed guidelines would focus on establishing appropriate guardrails for AI use, including disclosures, accountability of regulated entities and a 'human-in-the-loop' approach to ensure that critical decisions are subject to human oversight.In June 2025, Sebi floated a consultation paper proposing guiding principles for responsible usage of Artificial Intelligence (AI)/ Machine Learning (ML) applications/models in securities markets.These guiding principles are intended to optimise benefits and minimise potential risks associated with the integration of AI/ML based applications in securities markets to safeguard investor protection, market integrity, and financial stability.Speaking at the inauguration of Sebi's pavilion at the 45th India International Trade Fair (IITF) 2026, organised by the India Trade Promotion Organisation (ITPO), on Saturday, Pandey said the regulator has been continuously strengthening its cybersecurity framework to address rising cyber threats.He highlighted growing concerns over cyberattacks targeting financial institutions and cryptocurrency platforms, as well as digital frauds involving social media influencers.Following emerging threats, the regulator also introduced a structured incident response mechanism in May this year, aligned with the Financial Stability Board's FIRE reporting template, he said at the sidelines of an event here on Saturday.On quantum computing-related risks, the Chairman said Sebi is undertaking an inventory of cryptographic systems and identifying areas where cryptography is being used to assess potential vulnerabilities.He said markets globally are preparing for the risks posed by quantum computing, with concerns expected to become more pronounced around 2032-35, and stressed the need to complete preparations well in advance.On AI adoption, he said Sebi has also developed several supervisory tools, including its 'Sudarshan' tool, which is being demonstrated at international regulatory forums.The regulator is also working on strengthening its AI capabilities through international initiatives and supervisory toolkits, he added.The Chairman further said Sebi is reviewing the regulatory framework to ensure that the use of AI by market participants does not compromise investor protection, market safety or integrity.On startups and the listing framework, the Sebi chief also said the regulator has formed a working group to examine ways to make the Innovators Growth Platform (IGP) more attractive for startups, particularly deep-tech and biotech companies that require long gestation periods before generating profits.He said the existing platform has not gained the desired traction, and the regulator is reviewing potential changes to help such companies access public markets at an earlier stage.The objective is to provide investors clarity about the higher risks associated with such businesses while allowing them to participate in their long-term growth potential.However, he declined to share details of budget-related discussions.

The Department of Expenditure under the ministry has defined Abnormally Low Bids (ALBs) in government procurement, mandating scrutiny of bids falling below the prescribed threshold and seeking written clarifications wherever "concerns" arise over the bidder's ability to execute the contract at the quoted price.

articles.title: Ebola outbreak remains out of control in Congo 6 months into response
articles.summary:
Six months after an Ebola outbreak was declared in Congo, the disease remains out of control and efforts to contain it are faltering.
More than 11,000 cases have been recorded, and nearly half of those infected have died, according to government data. It is the deadliest of Congo's 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.
Basic containment measures, including contact tracing and isolation, remain inadequate, raising doubts about authorities' ability to halt the outbreak. Experts say there is little chance of bringing it under control within the next year.
By the time the outbreak was announced in mid-May, 43 deaths had already been recorded, suggesting the virus had circulated undetected for an extended period. It has since spread to eight of the country's 26 provinces, moving at a pace aid groups have likened to wildfire.

articles.summary:
India has voted against a draft UN General Assembly resolution calling on nations to establish a moratorium on the death penalty.
The 193-member UNGA adopted by recorded vote the resolution on Friday introduced by Mexico on 'Moratorium on the use of the death penalty', with 133 countries voting in favour of the resolution, 33 against and 16 abstentions.
India, along with Bahrain, China, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Japan, Kuwait, Maldives, Oman, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the US, voted against the resolution.
The resolution expressed deep concern about the continued application of the death penalty and reaffirmed the right of all countries to develop their own legal systems, including determining appropriate legal penalties in accordance with international law.
